source: Morewedge, Yoon, Scopelliti, Symborski, Korris, Kassam (2015) Debiasing decisions: improved decision making with a single training intervention
finding: A single serious game with personalised feedback and practice cut bias more than a training video, and the effect lasted months. This is the strongest human debiasing result in the literature.
numbers: Exp 1: 278 recruited, 243 finished lab, 196 did the 8-week follow-up (game n=160, video n=83). Bias blind spot, confirmation bias, fundamental attribution error. Games cut bias 46.25% right away and 34.76% at follow-up; videos 18.60% and 20.10%. Exp 2 (anchoring, representativeness, social projection, 12-week follow-up): games 31.94% then 23.57%; videos 25.70% then 19.20%.
quote: Games, which provided personalized feedback and practice, produced larger effects than did videos.
limits: Government-sponsored; measures are scale items close to the trained paradigms; game is proprietary; about 20% lost by follow-up. Later field transfer shown only in Sellier 2019 (same group).
agent_relevance: Feedback plus practice beat plain instruction. A scaffold that only tells the model to avoid bias is the video arm, not the game arm.

source: Morewedge, Yoon, Scopelliti, Symborski, Korris, Kassam (2015) Debiasing decisions: improved decision making with a single training intervention (transfer within a bias)
finding: Debiasing was domain-general within a bias: reduction showed on problem formats that were taught and ones that were not.
numbers: Gains held for trained and untrained facets of confirmation bias at posttest (trained facets larger: t(159)=2.56, p<.05). Knowledge of the biases also improved and persisted.
limits: Untrained facets still share the same bias construct; this is near transfer, not far transfer.
agent_relevance: Training on the structure of a bias, not its wording, is the target for any agent check.

source: Sellier, Scopelliti, Morewedge (2019) Debiasing training transfers to improve decision making in the field
finding: One-shot game training transferred to an unannounced business case (Carter Racing, a Challenger-style launch decision) with no reminder of bias.
numbers: N=290 graduate students (HEC Paris). Chose the inferior hypothesis-confirming race option: 58.8% trained vs 72.2% untrained (b=-.60, p=.022, odds ratio .55, CI .33-.92). Paper headline: 29% fewer. Windows around training: 2 days 50.0 vs 85.7%, 4 days 48.0 vs 76.0%, 6 days 48.0 vs 72.7%. Training lag averaged about 18 days. Trained students were less confident in their decision.
quote: Trained participants were 29% less likely to choose the inferior hypothesis-confirming solution
limits: Assignment by natural schedule, not random. Selection concerns tested with GPA, GMAT, CRT controls and short windows. One decision, one bias. Authors call it promising.
agent_relevance: A rare answer to the claim that training does not transfer to the field. Supports practice-with-feedback modules, tested on unseen tasks.

source: Sellier et al. (2019) mechanism and Hawthorne control
finding: A shift in confirmatory hypothesis testing (more disconfirming arguments) carried the effect; confidence did not.
numbers: Logistic model with confirming and disconfirming arguments as predictors: each argument type predicted racing in opposite directions. Adding confidence: confidence beta=.16, p=.053; training stayed beta=-.53, p=.047, odds ratio .59, CI .35-.99.
limits: Mediation by argument counts is correlational; the effect shrinks to borderline p when covariates are added.
agent_relevance: The useful step is a forced search for disconfirming evidence, not a generic be-careful line.

source: Heerma van Voss, Yoon, Scopelliti, Zweet, Helsloot, Morewedge (2025) Debiasing training reduces confirmation bias in national risk analysts
finding: A 40-minute one-shot training (scripted explanation plus Carter Racing group exercise) cut confirmation bias in experts and novices alike, a conceptual replication in a high-expertise sample.
numbers: 71 national risk analysts (56 valid) and 118 risk-policy master's students. Group effect F(1,169)=25.93, eta2=.133 (analysts less biased). Intervention effect F(1,169)=20.74, eta2=.109; no group by intervention interaction. Pre to post ANCOVA: general F(1,168)=104.58, eta2=.384; risk domain F=46.0, eta2=.215. Bias blind spot also fell (F(1,163)=5.72, eta2=.034).
limits: Posttest right after training, no delay. Pre-registered, but small expert N. Gains rest on pre-post change without an untrained control arm. Women improved more (p=.008).
agent_relevance: Expertise does not remove the gain from a debiasing step. Scale items are close to the training content, so effect sizes are likely upper bounds.

source: Heerma van Voss et al. (2025) bias blind spot and floor effect
finding: Everyone rated themselves less biased than others, experts too, and this did not predict real bias. The expected floor effect for experts did not appear.
numbers: Blind spot above 0 in all cells (analysts all M>0.968, students all M>0.894 on a -6 to 6 scale). Blind spot not correlated with confirmation bias (all r<.09 analysts, <.023 students). Pretest-adjusted posttest group difference not significant (general F(1,168)=1.21, p=.27; risk F=2.00, p=.159).
limits: Self-report scale; null correlations in small samples.
agent_relevance: Self-assessed I checked for bias is not evidence of being unbiased. The agent needs external checks, not its own confidence.

source: Soll, Milkman, Payne (2015) A user's guide to debiasing
finding: Review splits debiasing into modifying the person and modifying the environment. Training in normative rules fails when people have strong intuitions and do not pause; the best education is domain-specific and close in time to the decision.
numbers: As cited in the chapter: statistical-principle transfer fades over weeks (Fong and Nisbett 1991); meteorologists well calibrated in their domain are as poorly calibrated as others outside it (Keren 1991).
quote: Training in normative rules can fail when people have strong intuitions and do not pause to think more deeply
limits: Secondary summary; numbers sit in the cited papers.
agent_relevance: Matches the schema stance that generic checklists fail: tailor the check to the task and bias.

source: Soll, Milkman, Payne (2015) incentives and accountability
finding: Incentives and accountability help only when the bias comes from too little effort. They can backfire when effort goes into a wrong model.
numbers: As cited: incentivised judges who tried to improve on a reliable formula with their own knowledge did worse than unrewarded ones (Arkes, Dawes, Christensen 1986). Accountability reduces sunk-cost errors (Simonson and Nye 1992). Incentives lead people to think harder but not smarter (Larrick 2004).
limits: Review claims; the effort-versus-model-error split is a framework, not an effect size.
agent_relevance: Try-harder prompts or reward framing will not fix a wrong frame for an LLM; extra tokens in the same frame may not help.

source: Fischhoff (1982) Debiasing; Fong, Krantz, Nisbett (1986); Milkman, Chugh, Bazerman (2009), as summarised in Sellier 2019
finding: Older work found training works on the trained problem type but often fails to transfer unless it is extensive or people know they are tested. Fischhoff's four strategies: warnings, teaching direction of bias, feedback, extended coaching.
numbers: No numbers read directly. Sellier says early tests found transfer failed unless training was extensive (statistics courses) or trainees knew they were tested.
limits: Read only through the 2015 and 2019 papers.
agent_relevance: Warnings alone are the weakest rung; rely on structure and feedback loops.

source: Mellers, Stone, Atanasov, Rohrbaugh, Metz, Ungar, Bishop, Horowitz, Merkle, Tetlock (2015) The psychology of intelligence analysis
finding: In a two-year forecasting tournament, a short probabilistic-reasoning training (outside view, averaging, warnings about confirmation and hindsight bias) improved accuracy in a randomised design.
numbers: 743 forecasters, over 150,000 forecasts. Training vs accuracy r=.17 (t(741)=4.56); teaming r=.30. Regression on standardised Brier score with intelligence, open-mindedness, political knowledge, training and teams: R=.43 (F(5,587)=26.13). Year 1 was 3x3 (probability training, scenario training, none by independent, crowd-belief, team); year 2 kept only probability training and teams.
quote: Forecasters were warned against judgmental errors, such as wishful thinking, belief persistence, confirmation bias, and hindsight bias.
limits: Modest effect sizes; training was a bundle of tips, so no single component is isolated. Volunteers above average in education.
agent_relevance: Real-world evidence that a short outside-view and base-rate module raises forecast accuracy; fits an operator for reference classes and averaging.

source: Mellers et al. (2015) individual differences
finding: Dispositions mattered as much as training: open-minded style, intelligence and knowledge predicted skill, as did belief updating frequency and deliberation time.
numbers: Standardised betas: intelligence 0.18, political knowledge 0.15. Multiple R=.43.
limits: Observational for dispositions.
agent_relevance: Suggests small repeated belief updates and deliberate time matter more than one-pass answers.

source: Mellers et al. (2015) training module contents and scenario arm
finding: The module taught comparison classes, trend extrapolation, averaging estimates, validated models, and bias warnings. The scenario module (generate futures, decision trees, avoid overconfidence) was less effective and dropped.
numbers: Year 1 showed probabilistic-reasoning training was the most effective module; only it was kept for year 2.
limits: Bundle design.
agent_relevance: Outside view and averaging are concrete operators; scenario generation alone did less.

source: Aczel, Bago, Szollosi, Foldes, Lukacs (2015) Is it time for studying real-life debiasing? Analogical intervention technique
finding: Analogical training helped only for statistical-principle biases; for the other biases neither analogical nor awareness training gave gains at 4 weeks.
numbers: N=154, 10 biases (including anchoring, framing, sunk cost, overconfidence, planning fallacy), test before and 4 weeks after. Gain mainly on statistical biases, most on insensitivity to sample size. About twice as many in the analogical group said they used the strategies in daily life.
limits: Analogical group trained longer (time and interactivity confounded). Few items per bias. Authors call it an early step.
agent_relevance: Awareness training alone left most biases unchanged. Debiasing is bias-specific; one generic step will not cover all.

source: Aczel et al. (2015) rival accounts of why biases persist
finding: Two accounts compete: biases as storage, monitoring or inhibition failure (De Neys and Bonnefon 2013) versus missing mindware (Stanovich and West 2008). Training worked where the missing piece was an abstract rule.
numbers: Gain seen only for statistical biases that need a rule; no gain for biases that are mainly inhibition problems.
limits: No single experiment here separates the accounts.
agent_relevance: Pick the fix by cause: missing rule gets a reference or formula, missing check gets forced disconfirming search, wrong frame gets restart.

source: O'Sullivan and Schofield (2019) A cognitive forcing tool to mitigate cognitive bias: a randomised control trial
finding: A cognitive forcing checklist (the SLOW tool) did not reduce diagnostic error in bias-inducing vignettes, although doctors liked it.
numbers: 76 participants from student to attending. Mean cases correct 2.8 (tool) vs 3.1 (control), 95% CI -0.94 to 0.45, p=.49. Think-aloud with 20 doctors: first framing drove later errors; consider-the-opposite made clinical plans safer even when initial accuracy did not rise.
quote: insufficient evidence to recommend this tool in clinical practice
limits: Small volunteer sample; online vignettes; underpowered for small effects. Authors: insufficient evidence to recommend.
agent_relevance: Direct support for SCHEMA 4b: a checklist can feel useful and not move accuracy. Test each scaffold step by outcome.

source: Echterhoff, Liu, Alessa, McAuley, He (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Large models show patterns like human cognitive bias in admissions-style decisions; simple prompt fixes partly work or break instruction following.
numbers: 13,465 prompts; GPT-4, GPT-3.5-turbo, Llama-2 7B and 13B. Framing: GPT-4 admits 40.5% more students under the reject framing. Group attribution: Llama-2 7B classes 32.1% fewer females as good at math. Few-shot and counterfactual mitigation sometimes drove admission or rejection to nearly 0 or 100% (instruction failure). Self-help (model rewrites its own biased prompt) cut biased wording to 0% for group attribution in GPT-4 and 2.7% for framing.
limits: Admissions setting; 400 prompts per experiment; no human baseline on same items; Llama models changed 40-52% of anchoring decisions when asked to self-debias.
agent_relevance: Self-rewrite works for strong models and fails for weak ones. Examples can derail the task. Check each step for side effects.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) primacy and status-quo results
finding: Models prefer options shown first (A or B over C or D); status-quo wording inversely biased most models. Self-help gave the most even spread; awareness prompts helped a little.
numbers: Fraction choosing A or B exceeded C or D in all models; counterfactual and contrastive prompts made models ignore some options; Llama change rates when asked to self-debias: 0.399 (7B), 0.521 (13B); GPT-3.5 0.052, GPT-4 0.175.
limits: Figure-based results for several cells.
agent_relevance: Permute option order as a built-in step; do not rely on a be-neutral line.

source: Lyu, Ren, Feng, Wang, Chen, Ren, de Rijke (2025) Self-adaptive cognitive debiasing for LLMs in decision-making (SACD)
finding: A loop that finds the bias, analyses it, then rewrites the prompt, repeated until clean, beat zero-shot warnings, few-shot examples, CoT, Reflexion, multi-agent debate and self-help, especially with several biases at once.
numbers: Finance (FOMC), PubMedQA, LegalBench; llama3.1-8b and 70b, gpt-3.5-turbo, gpt-4o; 500 samples (100 for gpt-4o). Bias score = gap in choosing the biased option between biased and control prompts. FOMC llama3.1-8b: vanilla 0.3805, CoT 0.3425, zero-shot debias 0.2965, self-help 0.2100, SACD 0.1570. SACD averages: 0.03-0.157 FOMC, 0.0425-0.179 PubMedQA, 0.04-0.1235 LegalBench. Few-shot debiasing often above 0.5.
limits: Biases injected into prompts (anchoring, bandwagon, loss aversion); the score measures choice shift, not accuracy.
agent_relevance: Iterating detect, explain, rewrite beats one-pass reminders, but gain is measured on injected bias, not correctness.

source: Lyu et al. (2025) negative results for reflection and debate
finding: Reflexion and multi-agent debate raised bias; they reinforce bias from earlier turns or other agents.
numbers: Multi-agent debate on FOMC with gpt-3.5-turbo: average bias 0.5155. Reflexion on PubMedQA with llama3.1-70b: 0.5585. llama3.1-70b FOMC: vanilla 0.1648, few-shot 0.3655, few-shot debias 0.2900. CoT averages 0.247-0.615 across domains.
limits: Same injected-bias design.
agent_relevance: More agents or reflection is not less bias; a reviewer without an explicit bias check passes bias on.

source: Huang, Bie, Na, Ruan, Lei, Yue, He (2026) Understanding the anchoring effect of LLM with synthetic data (SynAnchors)
finding: Anchoring appears in all tested models and common mitigations remove at most about 10 points. Reasoning models show less.
numbers: Total anchored-answer ratio: Qwen2.5-0.5B 60.5%, Mistral-7B 51.1%, GPT-4o-mini 37.0%, GPT-4o 27.3%, DeepSeek-R1 25.0%, Qwen3-235B thinking 22.0%. Llama-3.1-8B baseline 34.7%: question-aware prompt 36.8%, self-improving 38.4%, knowledge enhancement 50.5%, adversarial LoRA 33.3%, DoLa 37.5-38.5%, Anti-DP (set own standard first, then rethink) 24.7%. Qwen2.5-7B baseline 40.0%, Anti-DP 40.8%.
limits: Synthetic data; two small target models; Anti-DP did not help Qwen on numeric tasks.
agent_relevance: Several popular prompt fixes made anchoring worse. Setting an independent standard first then reasoning helped on one model.

source: Lou and Sun (2024) Anchoring bias in large language models: an experimental study
finding: Strong models are pulled by expert anchor hints and cannot be corrected by asking them to ignore the hint, or by CoT, principles or reflection. Giving two different hints (both-anchor) helped.
numbers: 62 questions across domains; GPT-4 and GPT-4o. None of CoT, thoughts of principles, ignore-anchor, reflection effectively reduced anchoring. Example question 6: no-anchor answer 234,700 vs 522,600 with a CoT prompt plus anchor.
quote: none of these simple mitigating strategies can effectively reduce the anchoring bias
limits: Dataset from an earlier human study; two models; no significance tests seen in the text read.
agent_relevance: Matches human data: ignore it does not work. Supplying opposing views (consider-the-opposite style) is the lever.

source: Itzhak, Stanovsky, Rosenfeld, Belinkov (2024) Instructed to bias
finding: Instruction tuning and RLHF make models more biased on decoy effect, certainty effect and belief bias than their base versions.
numbers: GPT-3, Mistral and T5 families; Flan-T5, Mistral-Instruct, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 show stronger bias. In Mistral-Instruct belief bias is significantly lower and certainty bias higher.
limits: Three biases only; results depend on prompt format.
agent_relevance: Alignment training can add the biases a scaffold then has to remove. Re-test after any model switch.

source: Malberg, Poletukhin, Schuster, Groh (2025) A comprehensive evaluation of cognitive biases in LLMs
finding: Large benchmark: all 30 tested biases appear in at least some of 20 models.
numbers: 30,000 tests, 20 models, 30 biases. Average bias score per model 0.0 to 0.22; average absolute score 0.30-0.54. Framing about 0.41 and anchoring about 0.39 averaged across models (heatmap).
limits: Measures bias only; no mitigation arm in the part read.
agent_relevance: Anchoring and framing are strong; test them first.

source: Suri, Slater, Ziaee, Nguyen (2023) Do large language models show decision heuristics similar to humans?
finding: GPT-3.5 shows human-like heuristics on classic problems but is very sensitive to small prompt wording changes.
numbers: Authors state ChatGPT is remarkably sensitive to even small differences in prompts; GPT-4 tried on only a small number of trials.
limits: Few items; model often refuses money questions.
agent_relevance: Any bias test must vary wording; one prompt gives noisy results.

source: Jones and Steinhardt (2022) Capturing failures of large language models via human cognitive biases
finding: Code models (Codex, CodeGen) are pulled by anchor-like prompt features and make errors similar to human anchoring.
numbers: Prompts built from HumanEval and MathEquations; greedy decoding.
limits: Code tasks only; no debiasing method tested.
agent_relevance: An earlier wrong name or example in the prompt can steer output; shuffle or remove anchors.
